blocks.text:
This book has fourteen Parts and several hundred pages. Read front to back without a plan, most people stall around the collections chapters and never reach concurrency or the JVM, which are exactly the topics interviewers like. This chapter turns the book into a schedule: **25 study days spread over four weeks**, with a fixed daily loop, a checkpoint at the end of each week, and a list of what to skip if you are short of time.

The plan is deliberately **JVM first**. Java feels like a language, but it is really a language plus a runtime. Once you can picture the heap, the stack, class loading and the JIT, later topics (string pool, `HashMap` memory, thread visibility, garbage collection) stop being facts to memorise and become consequences you can derive.

### The daily loop

Every study day has the same three blocks. Keep the order; the third block is the one people skip and the one that makes the knowledge stick.

rows: Read the day's chapters once at normal speed. Do not type yet. Mark every sentence you could not explain to a friend.
Re-type the listings (do not paste). Change one thing in each and predict the result before you run it. Use `jshell` for one-liners.
Close the book. Answer the chapter's Check yourself questions from memory, then the matching quiz from the last Part of this book. Write wrong answers in your error log.
blocks.caption: The daily loop (about 100 to 110 minutes).

blocks.text:
#### The error log

Keep a plain text file called `errors.txt`. For every question you get wrong, write one line: the topic, what you answered, the correct idea in your own words. At the end of each week re-read only this file. It is a few pages long and it is a map of your personal weak spots, which is far more valuable than another pass through material you already know.

#### Rules that keep the plan honest

- Typing beats reading. A listing you have re-typed and changed is remembered; a listing you have scrolled past is not.
- Predict, then run. Before you execute any program, write down what you think it prints. A wrong prediction is the most useful event in the whole session.
- Do not move on with an unexplained term. If "happens-before" or "type erasure" is still fuzzy, spend ten minutes with the chapter's examples before the next day starts.
- One missed day is fine. Two in a row means you drop the lowest-priority item of the next day (see the skip list below), not that you cram.

### Weekly checkpoints

At the end of each week, spend 30 minutes on these tests before you continue. If you fail more than a quarter of a checkpoint, repeat that week's weakest day instead of starting the next week.

### If you are short of time

Not everyone has 25 free days. Here is what to cut, in the order to cut it. Never cut the Check yourself blocks; cut reading breadth first.

rows: Everything in the plan, one chapter per block
Skip Part 5 serialization and properties, the unicode chapter, Part 10 reflection and modules, Part 11 build tools

All of Parts 4 (except strings), 5 (except exceptions), 10, 11, 12; read only the Q&A of Part 14

Everything else; use the cheat sheets in the next chapter as your notes

blocks.text:
Whatever you skip, do not skip Part 13. A project that you built, ran and can explain is worth more in an interview than any number of memorised answers.

### Tracking progress

Pick one method and use it every day; the method matters less than the habit.

- **A grid.** Draw 25 boxes on paper and tick one each day you finish all three blocks. A streak you can see is motivating.
- **A score sheet.** After each quiz, write the date and score. Re-take any quiz scoring below 9 of 12 three days later without looking at the answers.
- **A GitHub repository.** Create one repository with a folder per Part and commit every listing you re-typed, with your own changes. In an interview it shows real practice, and it gives you something concrete to talk about.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "How did you learn Java?" A strong answer is specific: "I studied the JVM first, then rebuilt each concept in code. For example, I broke `hashCode` on purpose to see a `HashMap` degrade, reproduced a lost update with `count++`, and read GC logs from a program I made allocate heavily." Concrete experiments are far more convincing than a list of books or courses.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Study in the same place at the same time each day. A fixed slot removes the daily decision "should I study today", which is the real enemy of a 25-day plan.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Plan: 25 days, four weeks, JVM first.

- Daily loop: read 40 minutes, code 40 minutes, test 20 to 30 minutes. The test block is not optional.
- Keep an error log and re-read it weekly; it is a personal map of weak spots.
- Use the four weekly checkpoints; repeat a weak day rather than rush on.
- If short of time, cut breadth (serialization, modules, build tools) but never the projects or the Check yourself blocks.

These tables are meant to be scanned, not read. They compress the book into reference pages you can review the night before an interview or keep open while coding. Each sheet names the Part where the details live. A cheat sheet is a memory aid, not a teacher: if a row surprises you, go back to the chapter.

### Keywords and modifiers

Java has about 50 reserved keywords (including `const` and `goto`, which are reserved but unused), plus the literals `true`, `false`, `null`. Words such as `var`, `record`, `sealed`, `permits`, `yield` and `when` are *contextual* keywords: special only in some positions, still legal as variable names in most places (`var` and `yield` cannot be type names).

blocks.text:
### Primitive types and ranges

The ranges are exact; the "about" values are for quick mental use. All integral types are signed except `char`.

Remember: `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` wraps to `Integer.MIN_VALUE`; `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative; `Math.addExact` throws instead of wrapping; `Integer` objects between -128 and 127 are cached, so `==` works there and nowhere else dependably; `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`, use `BigDecimal` for money.

### Operator precedence

From highest (binds first) to lowest. Operators on one row have equal precedence. When in doubt, add parentheses; readers will thank you.

Traps: `&&` binds tighter than `||`; `1 + 2 + "x"` is `"3x"` but `"x" + 1 + 2` is `"x12"`; compound assignment hides a cast (`byte b = 10; b += 5;` compiles); `%` keeps the sign of the dividend (`-7 % 3` is `-1`).

### Collections: Big-O and when to use

n is the number of elements. "Amortised" means averaged over many operations. Hash costs assume a decent `hashCode`; a bad one degrades toward O(n) (O(log n) after treeification).

rows: Default list; random access, mostly appending
blocks.caption: Time complexity of common operations (Part 6).

blocks.text:
Decision shortcuts: need key to value lookup, use `HashMap`; need it sorted, `TreeMap`; need insertion order, `LinkedHashMap`; need a queue or stack, `ArrayDeque`; need unique elements, `HashSet`; need immutable, `List.of`, `Set.of`, `Map.of` (no nulls, unmodifiable). `HashMap` defaults: capacity 16, load factor 0.75, a bucket becomes a tree at 8 entries when the table has at least 64 slots, and goes back to a list at 6.

### Stream operations

A stream pipeline is source, zero or more intermediate operations (lazy), one terminal operation (triggers the work). A stream can be consumed once (Part 7).

blocks.text:
### The java.util.function interfaces

Learn the pattern, not 43 names: a function consumes (`Consumer`), produces (`Supplier`), tests (`Predicate`), transforms (`Function`), or combines (`BiFunction`). Prefixes `Bi` (two arguments), `Unary` and `Binary` (same type in and out), and `Int`, `Long`, `Double` (primitive specialisations that avoid boxing) modify them.

Method references come in four kinds: static (`Integer::parseInt`), bound instance (`System.out::println`), unbound instance (`String::length`), constructor (`ArrayList::new`). Captured local variables must be effectively final.

### Concurrency toolbox chooser

Start from the problem, not the class. Prefer the highest-level tool that solves it (Part 8).

rows: A flag seen by other threads
`new Thread` per task, unbounded `newCachedThreadPool` under load
Wait for N events / start together
pooling virtual threads; long `synchronized` blocks on Java 21
blocks.caption: Which tool for which problem.

blocks.text:
Golden rules: prefer immutability; confine mutable state to one thread when possible; always acquire locks in a fixed global order; never call unknown code while holding a lock; always shut executors down; treat `InterruptedException` as a request to stop, and restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` if you cannot rethrow.

### JVM flags

Flags starting with `-X` are standard-ish and stable; `-XX:` are HotSpot options (`+` turns a boolean on, `-` off, `=` sets a value). Defaults below were checked with `-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal` on JDK 21 on the build machine and depend on the machine.

blocks.text: "Which exception does each of these throw?" Practise saying, without hesitating: `1 / 0` throws `ArithmeticException`, but `1.0 / 0` is `Infinity` and no exception; `List.of(1).add(2)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`; `Integer x =` `null; int y = x;` throws `NullPointerException`; `Object o = "s"; Integer i = (Integer) o;` throws `ClassCastException`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Reference sheets for the whole book.

- Know the ranges: `int` is about 2.1e9, `long` about 9.2e18, `char` is unsigned 16 bits; overflow wraps silently.
- Pick collections by access pattern: `HashMap` for lookup, `TreeMap` for sorted, `ArrayDeque` for queues, `ArrayList` as the default list.
- Streams are lazy until a terminal operation; match the functional interface to the job (consume, produce, test, transform).
- Choose the highest-level concurrency tool that fits; use atomics, locks, queues and executors before raw `wait`/`notify`.
- For a live JVM, `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`, `GC.heap_info` and `GC.class_histogram` answer most first questions.

Reading feels like learning; recalling is learning. Each quiz below covers one Part of the book with twelve questions: a mix of multiple choice (A to D) and short answer, with tiny code snippets. Do them closed-book, write your answers down, and only then read the answers section that follows each quiz. Every snippet in these quizzes was compiled and run with JDK 21, and the printed results come from those runs. How to score: one point per question. Eleven or twelve means move on. Nine or ten means re-read the explanations you missed and add them to your error log. Eight or fewer means go back to that Part's chapter and redo its code block. Questions marked "short" want one or two sentences, not an essay. ### Quiz 1: The Java Platform and the JVM 1. (MC) Which of these contains the `javac` compiler? A) JRE B) JDK C) JVM D) JIT 2. (MC) What actually executes the contents of a `.class` file? A) the operating system directly B) the JVM (interpreter plus JIT compiler) C) `javac` D) the class loader 3. (short) Name the three phases of class loading and what the middle phase does. 4. (MC) Which runtime area is private to each thread? A) heap B) Metaspace C) JVM stack D) code cache 5. (short) State the class loader delegation rule in one sentence. 6. (MC) The file `Main.java` contains `class Main { public static void main(String[] args) {` `System.out.println(args.length); } }`. What does `java Main.java a "b c"` print? A) 0 B) 2 C) 3 D) a compile error 7. (MC) What does `java Hello.java` (Java 11 and later) do? A) Fails: you must run `javac` first B) Compiles in memory and runs the program C) Interprets the source text line by line D) Downloads the dependencies 8. (MC) Which release is not a long-term-support (LTS) release? A) 11 B) 17 C) 22 D) 25 9. (short) What replaced PermGen in Java 8, and where does it live? 10. (MC) Which statement about the JIT compiler is true? A) It compiles every method before the program starts B) It compiles frequently executed methods to machine code while the program runs C) It converts Java source to bytecode D) It is only used by the garbage collector 11. (short) What does `javap -c -p Foo` show that `javap Foo` does not? 12. (short) Where do local variables of primitive type, objects, and `static` fields live? #### Answers: Quiz 1 1. B. The JDK ships `javac`, `jar`, `jshell` and the tools; the JRE (runtime only) is no longer shipped separately by most vendors. 2. B. The JVM interprets bytecode and the JIT compiles hot code to machine code. 3. Loading, linking, initialisation. Linking has three steps: verify the bytecode, prepare (allocate and default static fields), resolve symbolic references. 4. C. Each thread has its own JVM stack (and PC register); heap, Metaspace and code cache are shared. 5. A loader first asks its parent to load the class and only tries itself if the parent cannot. 6. B. `args.length` is 2 (`a` and `b c`; the quotes make one argument). Verified by running. 7. B. The source launcher compiles in memory and runs it; no `.class` file is written. 8. C. The LTS releases are 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25. 9. Metaspace, in native (off-heap) memory, holding class metadata. 10. B. It profiles at run time and compiles hot methods (C1 first, then C2). 11. `-c` prints the bytecode instructions, `-p` includes private members. 12. Primitive locals live in the stack frame of the running method, objects on the heap, and `static` fields belong to the class (class-level data, not to any object). ### Quiz 2: Language Fundamentals 1. (what prints) `int x = 5; x = x++ + ++x; System.out.println(x);` 2. (what prints) `System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);` 3. (what prints) `byte b = 120; b += 10; System.out.println(b);` 4. (what prints) `char c = 'a'; c += 1; System.out.println(c); System.out.println(c + 1);` 5. (what prints) `System.out.println((int) 3.99 + " " + (byte) 200 + " " + 7 / 2 + " " + -7 % 3);` 6. (what prints) `System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1);` 7. (MC) What does `System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)` print? A) true B) false C) compile error D) 0.3 8. (short) What do `1.0 / 0` and `1 / 0` do? 9. (what prints) `System.out.println((5 > 3) ? 1 : 2.0);` 10. (short) Which keyword gives a value back from a block in a `switch` expression? 11. (short) What is the default value of each element of `new boolean[2]`, and what does `a[3] = 1` throw when `int[]` `a = new int[3]`? 12. Given overloads `g(int)`, `g(long)`, `g(Integer)` and `g(int...)`, what do `g((short) 5)`, `Integer boxed = 5;` `g(boxed)` and `g()` print, in that order? #### Answers: Quiz 2 1. 12. `x++` yields 5 (x becomes 6), `++x` makes it 7 and yields 7; 5 + 7 = 12. 2. `3345`. Evaluation is left to right: `1 + 2` is 3, then `"3"` makes the string `"33"`, then `4` and `5` are appended. 3. -126. `b += 10` is `b = (byte)(b + 10)`; 130 wraps to -126. 4. `b` and `99`. `c += 1` keeps type `char`; `c + 1` is an `int` (98 + 1). 5. `3 -56 3 -1`. Casting double to int truncates, 200 wraps to -56 as a byte, integer division truncates, and `%` takes the sign of the left operand. 6. -2147483648. Overflow wraps silently. 7. B. `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point. 8. `1.0 / 0` is `Infinity` (no exception); `1 / 0` throws `ArithmeticException: / by zero`. 9. `1.0`. The two branches are promoted to a common type, `double`. 10. `yield`. 11. A `boolean` array element defaults to `false`; `a[3] = 1` on a 3-element array throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. 12. `int`, `Integer`, `varargs`. For `(short) 5` widening to `int` wins over boxing and varargs; the phases are widening, then boxing, then varargs. Verified by running. ### Quiz 3: Object-Oriented Java 1. (what prints) A class has `static { System.out.print("S "); }`, an instance block `{ System.out.print("I "); }` and a constructor printing `"C "`. What does `new Init(); new Init();` print? 2. (what prints) With overloads `f(Object o)` and `f(String s)`, what does `f(null)` call? 3. (what prints) `class A { String n = "A"; String who() { return "A"; } } class B extends A { String n =` `"B"; String who() { return "B"; } }` Then `A a = new B(); System.out.println(a.n + " " + a.who());` 4. (what prints) A class `P` overrides `equals` (same `x` means equal) but not `hashCode`. After adding two `new P(1)` to a `HashSet

`, what is `size()`? 5. (what prints) `Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;` What do `a == b`, `c == d` and `c.equals(d)` print? 6. (what prints) With `record Pt(int x, int y) {}`, what does `System.out.println(new Pt(1, 2).equals(new` `Pt(1, 2)) + " " + new Pt(1, 2));` print? 7. (what prints) `Object o = "text"; String d = switch (o) { case Integer n -> "int"; case String s when` `s.length() > 3 -> "long str"; case String s -> "str"; default -> "other"; };` What is `d`? 8. (MC) Which members can an interface contain since Java 9? A) only abstract methods B) default, static and private methods C) instance fields D) constructors 9. (MC) Which statement about enums is true? A) An enum can extend another class B) An enum can implement interfaces C) An enum can have a public constructor D) Enums cannot have methods 10. (short) State the difference between overloading and overriding, including when each is resolved. 11. (short) Why must you override `hashCode` whenever you override `equals`? 12. (short) What does `sealed ... permits` buy you with `switch`? #### Answers: Quiz 3 1. `S I C I C` . The static block runs once at class initialisation; the instance block and constructor run for each object. 2. The `String` overload: the most specific applicable method is chosen at compile time. 3. `A B`. Fields are hidden, not overridden, and are resolved by the static type (`A`); methods are resolved dynamically by the runtime type (`B`). 4. 2 (almost certainly). Equal objects have different identity hash codes, so they land in different buckets; this breaks the contract. 5. `true false true`. Values from -128 to 127 are cached by `Integer.valueOf`; 128 creates distinct objects. 6. `true Pt[x=1, y=2]`. Records generate value-based `equals` and `toString`. 7. `long str`. Guards (`when`) refine a pattern; order matters, and the more specific case comes first. 8. B. Interfaces can have default, static and private methods, and constants, but no instance fields or constructors. 9. B. Enums implicitly extend `java.lang.Enum`, so they cannot extend a class; constructors are implicitly private. 10. Overloading: same name, different parameter lists, chosen at compile time from static types. Overriding: a subclass replaces an inherited instance method with the same signature, chosen at run time from the object's actual class. 11. The contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes. Otherwise hash-based collections look in the wrong bucket and treat equal objects as different. 12. The compiler knows every permitted subtype, so a `switch` over the type can be exhaustive without `default`, and adding a new subtype produces compile errors where you forgot to handle it. ### Quiz 4: Strings, Text and Time 1. (what prints) `String s1 = "hi", s2 = "hi", s3 = new String("hi");` What do `s1 == s2`, `s1 == s3`, `s1 ==` `s3.intern()` and `s1.equals(s3)` print? 2. (what prints) `System.out.println("a" + "b" == "ab");` and then `String ab = "a"; System.out.println(ab +` `"b" == "ab");` 3. (what prints) `new BigDecimal("1.10").equals(new BigDecimal("1.1"))` and `new` `BigDecimal("1.10").compareTo(new BigDecimal("1.1"))` 4. (what prints) `System.out.println(LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31).plusMonths(1));` 5. (what prints) `"a,b,,".split(",").length` 6. (what prints) `String s = "x"; s.concat("y"); System.out.println(s);` 7. (what prints) `String e = "\uD83D\uDE00"; System.out.println(e.length() + " " + e.codePointCount(0,` `2));` (this pair of escapes is one smiley character, outside the Basic Multilingual Plane) 8. (MC) `StringBuffer` differs from `StringBuilder` in that: A) it is synchronized B) it is immutable C) it is faster D) it supports Unicode only 9. (short) Why should you write `new BigDecimal("0.1")` and not `new BigDecimal(0.1)`? 10. (MC) Which java.time type represents a point on the machine timeline, independent of time zone? A) `LocalDateTime` B) `ZonedDateTime` C) `Instant` D) `Period` 11. (what prints) `Duration.ofMinutes(90)` and `Period.ofDays(10)` converted with `toString`. 12. (MC) Which formatter is safe to share between threads? A) `SimpleDateFormat` B) `DateTimeFormatter` C) both D) neither #### Answers: Quiz 4 1. `true false true true`. Literals share one pooled object; `new String` makes a separate object; `intern()` returns the pooled one. 2. `true`, then `false`. The first is a compile-time constant folded to the literal `"ab"`; the second concatenates at run time and creates a new object. 3. `false` and `0`. `equals` compares scale too (1.10 versus 1.1); `compareTo` compares numeric value. 4. `2024-02-29`. The day is clamped to the last valid day of the month (2024 is a leap year). 5. 2. Trailing empty strings are removed by `split`, leaving `a` and `b`. 6. `x`. Strings are immutable; the result of `concat` was discarded. 7. `2 1`. `length()` counts UTF-16 code units (a surrogate pair); one code point. 8. A. Both have the same API; `StringBuffer` synchronizes every method and is rarely needed. 9. `new BigDecimal(0.1)` captures the exact binary approximation of the double (0.1000000000000000055...); the string constructor gives exactly 0.1. 10. C. `Instant` is a count from the epoch; the others carry local fields or a zone. 11. `PT1H30M` and `P10D`. `Duration` is time-based, `Period` is date-based. 12. B. `DateTimeFormatter` is immutable and thread-safe; `SimpleDateFormat` is not. ### Quiz 5: Exceptions, I/O and Utilities 1. (what prints) `static int fin() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }` and `static int fin2() { int` `x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 5; } }`. What do `fin()` and `fin2()` return? 2. (what prints) A class `R implements AutoCloseable` prints `open1` or `open2` in its constructor and `close1` or `close2` in `close()`. What is printed by `try (R r1 = new R("1"); R r2 = new R("2")) { System.out.print("body "); }`? 3. (what prints) `System.out.println(Path.of("/a/b/../c").normalize());` 4. (what prints) What does `e.getMessage()` return when you catch the `NumberFormatException` from `Integer.parseInt("12x")`? 5. (MC) Which of these is a checked exception? A) `NullPointerException` B) `IOException` C) `ArithmeticException` D) `StackOverflowError` 6. (short) Why is `catch (Exception e) { }` with an empty body considered harmful? 7. (MC) What happens with `catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e)`? A) It works B) Compile error: the alternatives are related by subclassing C) Only the first is caught D) Runtime error 8. (short) What is a suppressed exception and how do you read it? 9. (MC) Why is Java's built-in serialization considered a security risk? A) It is slow B) Deserializing untrusted bytes can run attacker-chosen code paths C) It needs a database D) It only works on Windows 10. (short) Which method reads a file line by line lazily, and what must you do with the result? 11. (MC) You start a program with `java -Dmode=fast App`. How does the code read the value? A) `System.getenv("mode")` B) `System.getProperty("mode")` C) `args[0]` D) `Runtime.mode()` 12. (what prints) `int x = -1; assert x > 0 : "neg"; System.out.println("ran");` is run as `java N.java`. What happens, and what changes with `-ea`? #### Answers: Quiz 5 1. `2` and `1`. A `return` in `finally` overrides the earlier return (and swallows exceptions; never do it). In `fin2` the return value `1` was already evaluated before `finally` changed `x`. 2. `open1 open2 body close2 close1` . Resources are closed in reverse order of creation. 3. `/a/c`. `normalize()` removes `.` and `..` segments lexically. 4. `For input string: "12x"`. 5. B. `IOException` is checked. `StackOverflowError` is an `Error`; the others are unchecked. 6. It hides failures: the program continues in an unknown state and nobody learns why. Catch specific exceptions, handle them or rethrow, and at minimum log with the stack trace. 7. B. Verified by compiling: "Alternatives in a multi-catch statement cannot be related by subclassing". 8. When a resource's `close()` throws while another exception is already propagating, the close exception is attached to the primary one. Read it with `getSuppressed()`; stack traces show it as "Suppressed:". 9. B. The deserializer constructs objects from the byte stream, so crafted data can chain existing classes into harmful behaviour (gadget chains). Prefer JSON or records and use an `ObjectInputFilter` if you must deserialize. 10. `Files.lines(path)`. It returns a `Stream` that holds the file open, so close it with try-with-resources. 11. B. `-D` defines a system property. `getenv` reads environment variables, and `args` holds program arguments after the class name. 12. It prints `ran`, because assertions are disabled by default. With `java -ea N.java` it throws `AssertionError: neg`. Verified by running. ### Quiz 6: Generics and Collections 1. (what prints) `Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3).add(4);` What happens? 2. (what prints) `List l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3)); l.remove(1);` prints `[1, 3]`. What does `l.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` leave on a fresh `[1, 2, 3]`, and why is the first call different? 3. (what prints) `for (Integer v : list) if (v == 1) list.remove(v);` on `[1, 2, 3]` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. What happens if the test is `v == 2` instead, and what is the final list? 4. (what prints) `List ls = new ArrayList<>(); List raw = ls; raw.add(1); String s = ls.get(0);` Which line fails and with what? 5. (what prints) `TreeSet ts = new TreeSet<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER); ts.add("a");` `ts.add("A"); System.out.println(ts);` 6. (what prints) `Bad` has a `hashCode` based on mutable `v` and an `equals` on `v`. After `m.put(k, "v"); k.v = 2;` with `k.v` originally 1, what do `m.get(k)`, `m.get(new Bad(1))` and `m.size()` return? 7. (MC) Which line throws? A) `List.of(1, null)` B) `new ArrayList<>().add(null)` C) `new HashMap<>().put(null,` `1)` D) `new ArrayDeque<>().add(null)`. Pick every one that throws `NullPointerException`. 8. (what prints) `Deque dq = new ArrayDeque<>(); dq.push(1); dq.push(2); dq.addLast(3);` What does `System.out.println(dq + " " + dq.pop());` print? 9. (what prints) `PriorityQueue pq = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 3));` What do two successive `pq.poll()` calls return? 10. (what prints) `List src = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4)); src.subList(1, 3).set(0,` `99);` What is `src` now? 11. (MC) `HashMap` defaults are: A) capacity 10, load factor 0.5 B) capacity 16, load factor 0.75 C) capacity 16, load factor 1.0 D) capacity 8, load factor 0.75 12. (short) State PECS and name one method signature that uses it. #### Answers: Quiz 6 1. It throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. `Arrays.asList` is a fixed-size view of the array: `set` works, `add` and `remove` do not. 2. `[2, 3]`. `remove(int index)` is chosen for the literal `1` (it removes the element at index 1, leaving `[1, 3]`); `remove(Object)` is chosen for the boxed `Integer`. 3. Nothing is thrown, and the list ends as `[1, 3]`. After removing the second-to-last element, `hasNext()` sees `cursor` `== size` and the loop ends before `next()` checks for modification. This is a famous quirk, not a safe pattern. Use `removeIf` or an explicit `Iterator`. 4. The last line: `ls.get(0)` throws `ClassCastException` because the compiler inserts a cast to `String`. The raw `add` only produced a compiler warning (heap pollution). 5. `[a]`. The comparator treats `A` and `a` as equal, so the set rejects the second add. 6. `null`, `null`, `1`. The entry sits in the bucket for hash 1; looking up `k` now hashes to 2, and looking up `new Bad(1)` finds the entry but `equals` fails because the stored key now has `v == 2`. The entry is unreachable. Never mutate keys. 7. A and D throw. `List.of` rejects nulls and `ArrayDeque` forbids null elements; `ArrayList` and `HashMap` allow them. 8. `[2, 1, 3] 2`. `push` adds at the head; `pop` removes from the head. String concatenation evaluates `dq` first, then `pop()`. 9. `1` then `3`. A priority queue returns the smallest element first (natural order). 10. `[1, 99, 3, 4]`. `subList` is a view backed by the original list. 11. B. Capacity 16 and load factor 0.75 (resize at 12 entries). 12. "Producer extends, consumer super": use `? extends T` to read from a structure, `? super T` to write into it. Example: `static void copy(List dest, List src)`. ### Quiz 7: Functional Java: Lambdas and Streams 1. (what prints) `Stream.of(1, 2, 3).peek(v -> System.out.print("peek" + v + " ")).filter(v -> v > 1);` and nothing else. What is printed? 2. (what prints) `Stream.of(1, 2, 3).peek(v -> System.out.print("p" + v + " ")).filter(v -> v >` `1).findFirst().ifPresent(v -> System.out.println("found " + v));` 3. (what prints) `Stream.of("a", "bb", "cc").collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length))` 4. (what prints) `Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(v -> v % 2 == 0))` 5. (what prints) `Stream st = Stream.of(1); st.count(); st.count();` What happens on the second call? 6. (what prints) `Optional.of(null)` versus `Optional.ofNullable((String) null).orElse("x")`. 7. (what prints) `Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).reduce(10, Integer::sum)` and `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).sum()` 8. (what prints) `Stream.of("a", "a").collect(Collectors.toMap(v -> v, v -> 1))`: what happens? 9. (what prints) `Function inc = q -> q + 1, dbl = q -> q * 2;` What do `inc.andThen(dbl).apply(3)` and `inc.compose(dbl).apply(3)` return? 10. (MC) `int count = 0; list.forEach(x -> count++);` fails because: A) `forEach` is not allowed B) captured local variables must be effectively final C) `count` is a primitive D) lambdas cannot return void 11. (short) When is `orElseGet(supplier)` better than `orElse(value)`? 12. (short) How does the JVM implement a lambda: anonymous inner class or something else? #### Answers: Quiz 7 1. Nothing. Intermediate operations are lazy and there is no terminal operation, so `peek` never runs. 2. `p1 p2 found 2`. Elements flow one at a time, and `findFirst` short-circuits as soon as 2 passes the filter, so 3 is never touched. 3. `{1=[a], 2=[bb, cc]}`. 4. `{false=[1, 3, 5], true=[2, 4]}`. `partitioningBy` always has both keys. 5. `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`. A stream is one-shot. 6. `Optional.of(null)` throws `NullPointerException`; the second expression gives `x`. 7. `20` (10 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4) and `15`. 8. `IllegalStateException: Duplicate key a (attempted merging values 1 and 1)`. Pass a merge function as the third argument to handle duplicates. 9. `8` and `7`. `andThen` applies `inc` first ((3 + 1) \* 2); `compose` applies `dbl` first (3 \* 2 + 1). 10. B. Verified by compiling: "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final". Use an `AtomicInteger`, or better, a stream `count()`. 11. When computing the default is expensive or has side effects: `orElse` evaluates its argument always, `orElseGet` only when the `Optional` is empty. 12. Neither as an inner class file: the compiler emits an `invokedynamic` instruction and the `LambdaMetafactory` creates the implementing class at run time. `this` inside a lambda refers to the enclosing instance. ### Quiz 8: Concurrency 1. (short) Two threads each run `count++` 100,000 times on a shared `int`. Can the final value be less than 200,000? Why? 2. (what prints) `Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()));` `t.run();` What name is printed? 3. (what prints) `Thread tt = new Thread(() -> {}); tt.start(); tt.join(); tt.start();` What happens, and what is `tt.getState()` before `start`? 4. (what prints) `Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> {}); System.out.println(v.isDaemon());` 5. (what prints) `ConcurrentHashMap m = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); m.merge("a", 1,` `Integer::sum); m.merge("a", 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(m);` 6. (what prints) `AtomicInteger ai = new AtomicInteger(5); System.out.println(ai.getAndIncrement() + " "` `+ ai.incrementAndGet() + " " + ai.compareAndSet(7, 10) + " " + ai);` 7. (what prints) A thread runs `try { Thread.sleep(5000); } catch (InterruptedException e) {` `System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); }` and is interrupted from outside while sleeping. What is printed? 8. (what prints) `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 6).thenApply(q -> q * 7).get()` 9. (MC) `volatile` on an `int` field guarantees: A) atomic `x++` B) visibility of writes to other threads C) mutual exclusion D) a lock 10. (short) Name one way to avoid deadlock between two locks. 11. (MC) `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)` uses which queue? A) a bounded one of size 4 B) an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue` C) a `SynchronousQueue` D) none 12. (short) What does the Java Memory Model guarantee about `Thread.start()` and `Thread.join()`? #### Answers: Quiz 8 1. Yes. `count++` is read, add, write; two threads can read the same value and one update is lost. Fix with `AtomicInteger`, `synchronized` or a lock. 2. `main`. Calling `run()` executes the body on the calling thread. Only `start()` creates a new thread. 3. The second `start()` throws `IllegalThreadStateException`; before `start()` the state is `NEW` (after `join` it is `TERMINATED`). 4. `true`. Virtual threads are always daemon threads. 5. `{a=2}`. `merge` is atomic per key. 6. `5 7 true 10`. 7. `false`. When `InterruptedException` is thrown, the interrupt flag is cleared; call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` if you need to preserve it. 8. `42`. 9. B. `volatile` gives visibility and ordering, not atomicity of compound operations. 10. Always acquire locks in the same global order, or use `tryLock` with a timeout, or avoid holding two locks. 11. B. The unbounded queue means tasks pile up under load (a memory risk); for production, build a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded queue and a rejection policy. 12. Everything the starting thread did before `start()` happens-before the new thread's actions, and everything a thread did happens-before another thread's successful return from `join()` on it. ### Quiz 9: The JVM in Depth 1. (what prints) `try { long[] big = new long[Integer.MAX_VALUE]; } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) {` `System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }` What message appears on JDK 21? 2. (what prints) `static int depth = 0; static void rec() { depth++; rec(); }` Calling `rec()` inside `try { }` `catch (StackOverflowError e) { }` and then printing `depth > 1000` shows what? 3. blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
How to use the Part quizzes.

- Answer closed-book and in writing, then check; the effort of recalling is what builds memory.
- Score 11 or 12 and move on; 9 or 10, log the misses; 8 or fewer, redo that Part's code.
- For every wrong "what prints" answer, write the tiny program and run it. A run that surprises you is worth ten re-reads.
- Re-take any quiz you scored below 9 on after three days, without looking at the answers.

sections.title: Final Mock Interview and What to Do Next

blocks.text:
This is a single 60-question test that mixes everything. Treat it like a real interview: set a timer for **90 minutes**, close the book, and write your answers on paper. Snippets were compiled and run on JDK 21. Short-answer questions are marked (short); answer in one to three sentences, as you would speak in an interview. The key follows the questions.

Scoring: 52 to 60 means you are interview-ready on the fundamentals; 40 to 51 is solid, so review the topics of your misses; 30 to 39 means repeat weeks 2 to 4 of the study plan for your weak areas; below 30, go back to Part 1 and re-do the daily loop. Give half a point for a short answer that is right in spirit but vague.

### Round 1: Language and object-oriented Java

1. (what prints) `String s = null; s += "a"; System.out.println(s);`
2. (what prints) `int i = 0; i = i++; System.out.println(i);`
3. (what prints) `long l = Integer.MAX_VALUE * 2; System.out.println(l);`
4. (what prints) `System.out.println(Math.round(-2.5) + " " + Math.round(2.5));`
5. (what happens) `Integer n = null; int r = true ? n : 0;`
6. (what prints) `int x = 2; switch (x) { case 1: System.out.print("1"); case 2: System.out.print("2");` `case 3: System.out.print("3"); break; default: System.out.print("d"); }`
7. (what prints) `class Base { Base() { init(); } void init() { System.out.print("Base.init "); } }` and `class Derived extends Base { int v = 7; void init() { System.out.print("v=" + v + " "); } }`. What does `new Derived();` print?
8. (what happens) `interface X { default String n() { return "X"; } }` and `interface Y { default String` `n() { return "Y"; } }`. A class implements both. What must it do, and what does `X.super.n() + Y.super.n()` return?
9. (what prints) `float f = 0.1f; System.out.println(f == 0.1);`
10. (short) When do you choose an abstract class over an interface?
11. (MC) `final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` means: A) the list cannot change B) `names` cannot be reassigned, but the list can change C) the list is thread-safe D) the variable is a constant String
12. (short) What is a covariant return type? Give a one-line example.

### Round 2: Strings, exceptions and collections

1. (what prints) `Set<Short> ss = new HashSet<>(); for (short k = 0; k < 5; k++) { ss.add(k); ss.remove(k`

- `- 1); } System.out.println(ss.size());`

1. (what prints) `System.out.println(Arrays.asList(new int[]{1, 2}).size());`
2. (what prints) `System.out.println(new StringBuilder("a").equals(new StringBuilder("a")));`
3. (what happens) `Collections.sort(List.of(3, 1, 2));`
4. (what prints) `Map<String,Integer> m = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()); m.put("a", 1);` `m.put("c", 3); m.put("b", 2); System.out.println(m);`
5. (what prints) `System.out.println(new int[]{1}.equals(new int[]{1}) + " " + Arrays.equals(new` `int[]{1}, new int[]{1}));`
6. (what prints) `System.out.println(Objects.hash(1, 2, 3) + " " + List.of(1, 2, 3).hashCode());` Are the two numbers related?
7. (what prints) `System.out.println(String.valueOf((Object) null));`
8. (short) Why did Java's designers introduce checked exceptions, and what is the common criticism?
9. (short) What must a class implement to be used in try-with-resources?
10. (MC) Which allows a `null` key? A) `Hashtable` B) `ConcurrentHashMap` C) `HashMap` D) `TreeMap` with natural ordering
11. (short) When would you pick `LinkedList` over `ArrayList`?

### Round 3: Streams and concurrency

1. (what prints) `System.out.println(Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).skip(1).limit(2).toList());`
2. (what prints) `System.out.println(Stream.of("a", "b",` `"a").collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting())));`
3. (what prints) `List<Integer> li = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3)); li.removeIf(x -> x % 2 == 1);` `System.out.println(li);`
4. (what prints) `System.out.println(Optional.of(5).map(q -> q * 2).filter(q -> q > 20).isPresent());`
5. (what prints) `System.out.println(Long.valueOf(127) == Long.valueOf(127));`
6. (what prints) `System.out.println(Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).parallel().reduce(0, Integer::sum));` Is the result deterministic and why?
7. (short) Give two situations where a parallel stream is a bad idea.
8. (MC) `wait()` must be called: A) anywhere B) inside a `synchronized` block on the same object, ideally in a loop checking the condition C) only from the main thread D) after `notify()`
9. (short) Name two things `ReentrantLock` offers that `synchronized` does not.
10. (short) Why is `Executors.newCachedThreadPool()` risky under heavy load?
11. (short) When do virtual threads help, and when do they not?
12. (MC) Compared with `Collections.synchronizedMap`, `ConcurrentHashMap`: A) locks the whole map on each call B) allows concurrent updates and has atomic methods like `merge` C) keeps keys sorted D) is slower for all uses

### Round 4: JVM, memory and modern Java

1. (short) What is stored on the heap and what on a thread's stack?
2. (MC) `-Xmx2g` sets: A) the initial heap B) the maximum heap C) the stack size D) Metaspace limit

9. (what prints) `Object o = 42; if (o instanceof Integer n && n > 40) System.out.println(n + 1);`
10. (short) How does `sealed` help a `switch` expression?
11. (short) Name three features finalised in Java 21.
12. (MC) Java 25 is: A) a short-term release B) an LTS release C) preview only D) the first version with records

### Round 5: Mixed, design and tooling

1. (what prints) `System.out.println(Character.getNumericValue('7') + ('7' - '0') + " " + (char) ('a' +` `2));`
2. (what prints) `int[] arr = {3, 1, 2}; int[] cp = arr; Arrays.sort(cp); System.out.println(arr[0]);`
3. (what prints) `String t = "a"; t = t + 1 + 2; System.out.println(t);`
4. (what prints) `System.out.println(Integer.parseInt("-0") + Integer.valueOf("08"));`
5. (what prints) `double dd = 10; dd /= 4; int ii = 10; ii /= 4; System.out.println(dd + " " + ii);`
6. (short) What does the "D" in SOLID mean, and how do you apply it in plain Java?
7. (short) Name two problems with the classic singleton and one remedy.
8. (short) List the properties of the `equals` contract.
9. (short) Your service hangs and CPU is idle. How do you check for a deadlock?
10. (short) Why are immutable classes easier to use in concurrent programs?
11. (short) What is the role of a build tool like Maven or Gradle?
12. (short) Describe what happens inside `HashMap.get(key)`.

### Answer key

Questions 1 to 12:

1. `nulla`. `null + "a"` is string concatenation.
2. `0`. The old value is stored back after the increment, overwriting it.
3. `-2`. The multiplication happens in `int` and overflows before the widening to `long`.
4. `-2 3`. `Math.round` rounds half up (towards positive infinity).
5. `NullPointerException`: the conditional has type `int`, so `n` is unboxed.
6. `23`. Without `break`, execution falls through to the next case.
7. `v=0`. The superclass constructor runs before the subclass's field initialisers, so the overridden method sees the default 0. Never call overridable methods from a constructor.
8. The class must override `n()`, otherwise it does not compile. The expression gives `XY`.
9. `false`. `0.1f` widened to double is not 0.1.
10. When subclasses share state or constructor logic, you need non-public members, or you want a template method. Use an interface for a capability that unrelated classes may have; a class can implement many interfaces but extend one class.
11. B.
12. An overriding method may return a subtype of the overridden method's return type, for example `Object clone()` overridden as `Point clone()`.

Questions 13 to 24:

1. `5`. `k - 1` is an `int`, boxed to `Integer`, which never equals a `Short`, so `remove` removes nothing.
2. `1`. `asList` of an `int[]` produces a `List<int[]>` with a single element.
3. `false`. `StringBuilder` does not override `equals`; use `contentEquals` or `toString`.
4. `UnsupportedOperationException`; `List.of` is immutable.
5. `{c=3, b=2, a=1}`.
6. `false true`. Arrays use identity `equals`; `Arrays.equals` compares contents.
7. `30817 30817`. Both compute 31 \* h + element starting from 1, the `List` hash formula.
8. `null` (the text). `valueOf(Object)` returns the string "null".
9. To force callers to deal with recoverable failures. Criticism: they clutter code and leak implementation details across layers (lambdas and streams do not work well with them); many modern APIs and frameworks use unchecked exceptions.
10. `AutoCloseable` (or `Closeable`), with `close()`.
11. C. `Hashtable` and `ConcurrentHashMap` reject null keys, and a `TreeMap` with natural ordering throws on a null key.
12. Rarely. Mostly when you need constant-time insertion or removal through an iterator in the middle of a long list; for queues and stacks prefer `ArrayDeque`.

Questions 25 to 36:

1. `[2, 3]`.
2. `{a=2, b=1}`.
3. `[2]`.
4. `false`. 10 is not above 20.
5. `true`. `Long` caches -128 to 127 like `Integer`.
6. `21`. Deterministic, because addition is associative and the identity is 0; non-associative operations (such as subtraction) would give unpredictable results.
7. When tasks are tiny or the source is small (overhead dominates); when operations have side effects or touch shared mutable state; when tasks block on I/O (the common pool is small); when order matters and you rely on `forEach`.

10. It creates a new thread for every task when none is idle, with no upper bound, so a burst can exhaust memory or OS thread limits.

Questions 37 to 48:

1. Objects and arrays live on the heap (shared by all threads). Each thread's stack holds frames with local variables (primitives and references) and the operand stack.
2. B.
3. A minor collection cleans only the young generation (cheap and frequent, because most objects die young); a full collection processes the whole heap including the old generation and is more expensive.
4. Objects that stay reachable (so cannot be collected) although the program no longer uses them. Example: adding entries to a static `Map` cache and never removing them.
5. B.
6. C1 compiles quickly with light optimisation and profiling; C2 compiles hot code slowly with heavy optimisation (inlining, escape analysis) for peak speed. Tiered compilation uses both.

8. It cannot extend another class (it implicitly extends `Record`), cannot declare extra instance fields beyond its components, and its fields are final.

Questions 49 to 60:

1. `14 c`. 7 + 7 = 14, then the string concatenation; `'a' + 2` cast to `char` is `c`.
2. `1`. `cp` and `arr` are the same array; sorting through one is visible through the other.
3. `a12`. Left to right: `"a1"` then `"a12"`.
4. `8`. `-0` parses to 0 and `08` parses to 8 in `Integer.valueOf` (decimal, leading zero allowed).
5. `2.5 2`.
6. Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes. Apply it by declaring a field as an interface and passing the implementation in (constructor injection), as Spring does.
7. Global mutable state that is hard to test, and thread-safety or serialization/reflection issues. Remedy: use an `enum` singleton, or avoid the singleton and inject a single instance through a framework.
8. Reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent (same result while nothing changes), and `x.equals(null)` is false.
9. Take a thread dump with `jstack <pid>` or `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`; the JVM reports "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the threads and the locks they hold and wait for.

11. Dependency management, a standard project layout and lifecycle (compile, test, package), and reproducible builds from a declarative file (`pom.xml` or `build.gradle`).
12. Compute `hash(key)` (spread with `h ^ (h >>> 16)`), pick the bucket `(n - 1) & hash`, then walk the bucket's list or tree comparing hash and `equals`; return the value, or `null` if absent.

### What to do next

Finishing a book is the start of the work, not the end. Here is a sensible order for a Java backend career, based on how most interview loops and junior jobs look.

#### 1. Build and ship something (weeks 1 to 4)

Take one project from Part 13 and extend it: add a command-line interface, persistence with files, then a real database through JDBC. Put it on GitHub with a README that shows how to build and run it, a short design note and tests. Employers read repositories; one clear, working project beats several half-finished ones.

#### 2. Spring Boot (weeks 3 to 8)

Most Java backend jobs use Spring Boot. You are ready for it because you know the core ideas it relies on: reflection and annotations, dynamic proxies (for transactions and AOP), dependency injection (the Dependency Inversion principle), class loading, and threads. Learn in this order: a REST controller; dependency injection and beans; configuration properties; Spring Data JPA with a relational database; validation and error handling; testing with JUnit and `MockMvc`; then security basics. Use the official Spring guides and reference documentation, and rebuild your Part 13 project as a Spring Boot service.

#### 3. Data structures and algorithms (ongoing, 30 to 60 minutes a day)

Interviews for software engineers test problem solving in Java. Work through arrays and strings, hash maps and sets, two pointers and sliding window, stacks and queues, linked lists, recursion and backtracking, trees and graphs (BFS, DFS), heaps, binary search, and dynamic programming basics. For each problem, say the brute-force idea first, state its complexity, then improve it. Part 14 includes a set of coding problems with Java solutions as a starting point; the cheat sheet on collections tells you which structure gives the complexity you need.

#### 4. System design basics (after the above)

Learn to reason about a service rather than a class: client, load balancer, stateless application servers, cache, database, queue. Study relational versus NoSQL storage, indexing, replication and sharding, caching strategies and invalidation, message queues and eventual consistency, idempotency and retries, and observability (logs, metrics, traces). Practise by designing small things end to end, such as a URL shortener or a rate limiter, and always state requirements and trade-offs before drawing boxes.

#### 5. Keep the JVM skills alive

Read GC logs from a service you run, profile with JFR when something is slow, and read the release notes of each new Java version. The habit of testing a claim with a small program, which this book tried to teach, is the skill that keeps paying off.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Tell me about a project you built." Structure the answer: the goal, the design (two or three classes or components and why), one hard problem you hit and how you diagnosed it (a bug found with `jstack`, a performance problem found with a profiler, a race condition reproduced with a stress loop), and what you would improve. Concrete detail proves you did the work.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: After your mock interview, do not just read the key. For every miss, write a three-line program that proves the correct answer, run it, and add it to your repository as a note.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Final mock interview and next steps.

- The mock tests recall under time pressure; 52 or more of 60 means the fundamentals are in place.
- Convert every wrong answer into a runnable experiment and an entry in the error log.
- Next: one finished project on GitHub, Spring Boot, daily data-structures practice, then system design basics.
- Keep using the JVM tools (`jcmd`, `jstack`, GC logs, JFR); production debugging skill sets strong engineers apart.
#### The 25-Day, 4-Week Study Plan

items.question: Name the three blocks of the daily loop and say which one is most often skipped.
items.answer: Read, code, test. The test block (closed book, Check yourself plus quiz) is the one usually skipped.

items.question: Why does the plan start with the JVM instead of syntax?
items.answer: Many later topics (string pool, `HashMap`, memory visibility, GC) are consequences of how the JVM works; knowing the runtime lets you derive behaviour instead of memorising it.

items.question: What goes into the error log, and when do you re-read it?
items.answer: One line per wrong answer: topic, your answer, the correct idea in your own words. Re-read it at the end of each week and before the mock interview.

items.question: You have 10 days. Name two Parts you keep in full and two you cut.
items.answer: Keep Part 1 and Part 3 (also collections, concurrency basics, GC); cut Part 10 and Part 11 (also most of Parts 4, 5 and 12).

items.question: Week 3 checkpoint: you score 6 of 12 on the Part 7 quiz. What do you do?
items.answer: Below the pass mark, so repeat the weakest day (lambdas, Optional, streams or collectors, whichever the errors point to), then re-take the quiz three days later.

blocks.text: #### Cheat Sheets

items.question: What is `byte b = 120; b += 10;` followed by `System.out.println(b)`? Does it compile?
items.answer: It compiles, because compound assignment casts back to `byte`. 130 does not fit, so it wraps to -126.

items.question: A bucket in a `HashMap` holds 9 entries and the table has 16 slots. Does it become a tree?
items.answer: No. Treeification needs at least 8 entries in a bucket and a table of at least 64 slots; with fewer, `HashMap` resizes the table instead.

items.question: Which of `map`, `filter`, `sorted`, `count` are terminal operations?
items.answer: Only `count`. The other three are lazy intermediate operations.

items.question: You need a thread-safe counter incremented by 50 threads. Name the best tool and one wrong choice.
items.answer: `AtomicInteger` or `LongAdder`. A plain `int` or a `volatile int` with `count++` is wrong, because the increment is read, add, write and loses updates.

items.question: Which `jcmd` command lists how many instances of each class are alive?
Is `InterruptedException` checked or unchecked, and what do you do when you catch it and cannot rethrow?
items.answer: Checked. Restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` so callers can still see the interruption, then stop the work.
